selected_news.title: Afrika, COP31'de İklim Projeleri İçin Fon Talep Etti
selected_news.summary: As the curtains draw to a close on COP31 in Antalya, one question looms large for African countries: Will climate promises finally translate into the funding African communities need to cope with a warming world?
selected_news.source_headline: Africa at COP31: Will climate cash finally flow?
selected_news.article_text: For millions across the continent, climate change is no longer an abstract environmental concern debated in conference halls. It is already reshaping daily life, livelihoods and even decisions about where people can live In Zimbabwe, Harare resident Tsitsi Moyo says the effects are becoming increasingly difficult to ignore: "The extreme heat wave we have been experiencing I think also has issues to do with rainfall patterns." Jane Okello has witnessed similar changes in Uganda, describing increasingly erratic weather, including periods of unusually heavy rainfall associated with El Nino Their experiences reflect a wider trend across the continent. Communities that depend on predictable seasons for agriculture, water supplies and income are finding it harder to plan for the future as weather patterns become more extreme and less reliable To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video For some, the consequences go beyond disrupted harvests or shrinking water supplies. Climate pressures are also influencing migration patterns. According to Professor Alfred Ngomanda, permanent secretary of the Gabon Climate Council, environmental stress can push people to leave their homes in search of more favorable conditions and more secure livelihoods Climate change is rarely the sole reason people migrate. However, droughts, floods, declining agricultural output and other environmental strains often intensify existing economic and social challenges, making displacement more likely As African countries prepare to make their case at the climate negotiations, Ngomanda stressed that the continent must emphasize the global importance of its natural resources "We will go to Ethiopia [the host of COP32 in November 2027] to assert that the Congo Basin is a stabilizing element for the global climate, and not just for Africans," Ngomanda said At the heart of the discussions at COP31 is climate finance, the funding used to help countries reduce greenhouse gas emissions and adapt to the impacts of climate change COP, or the Conference of the Parties to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change, brings together governments from around the world to negotiate action on global warming. The talks build on the Paris Agreement, adopted at COP21 in 2015, which aims to keep global temperature rise well below 2 degrees Celsius while pursuing efforts to limit it to 1.5 degrees For African countries, the challenge is not simply making climate commitments, but securing the resources needed to turn those commitments into reality Opening the conference, United Nations (UN) Secretary-General Antonio Guterres highlighted what he described as a fundamental injustice in the global response to climate change "Developing countries face a double injustice: They bear the brunt of climate change but struggle to access the finance they urgently need," Guterres said The scale of the financing gap remains stark. According to the United Nations Economic Commission for Africa, the continent received about $52 billion (€44.5 billion) in climate finance in 2022, far short of its estimated annual requirement of $190 billion. Much of that funding also comes as loans, adding pressure to already strained public finances The shortfall is especially significant given that Africa contributes only about 4% of global greenhouse gas emissions, yet remains one of the regions most vulnerable to climate change African governments are therefore calling for funding that is more predictable, accessible and affordable, particularly for programs intended to help communities adapt to extreme weather, strengthen resilience and protect livelihoods African negotiators say the focus now must be on making sure that climate commitments produce tangible results on the ground. Speaking at a press conference on November 19, Veronica Nonhlanhla Jakarasi, lead negotiator for the African Group of Negotiators, argued that the continent needs a dedicated mechanism to translate climate proposals into funded projects "What we need is a mitigation implementation facility that moves Africa's proposals into actual financing and projects on the ground." She said such a facility would help direct more resources to the continent while supporting economic growth, green industrialization and the development of Africa's critical minerals sector without driving up emissions Mitigation focuses on reducing greenhouse gas emissions, while adaptation involves preparing for and responding to climate impacts. African countries insist both are essential if the continent is to pursue development while coping with increasingly severe weather events Negotiations remain difficult. A revised COP31 draft circulated on November 19, removed references to phasing out fossil fuels and dropped a proposed annual adaptation-finance target of $120 billion. While talks are ongoing and the text does not represent a final agreement, the changes underscore the political and financial battles that still shape international climate action For women like Moyo and Okello, however, the significance of COP31 will ultimately be measured far from the conference venue. Climate finance can support drought-resistant farming, improved water management systems, early-warning networks and infrastructure intended to withstand floods and extreme heat. But pledges alone will not deliver those outcomes. Countries must be able to access the money, implement projects effectively and ensure support reaches the communities that need it most To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Gerauds Wilfried Obangome contributed to this article

selected_news.shorts_hook: Afrika, iklim projeleri için yeni bir fon talep ediyor
selected_news.quality_hook: Afrika, iklim projeleri için yeni bir fon talep ediyor
selected_news.quality_narration: COP31'da Afrika Grubu müzakerecisi Veronica Nonhlanhla Jakarasi, kıtaya yönelik iklim projelerini finanse edecek bir ‘azaltma uygulama tesisi’ kurulması gerektiğini savundu. Jakarasi, bu mekanizmanın yeşil sanayileşme, kritik mineraller ve düşük emisyonlu büyüme hedeflerini destekleyeceğini belirtti. Aynı gün yayımlanan taslak, fosil yakıtların aşamalı olarak kaldırılmasına dair ifadeleri ve yıllık 120 milyar dolar uyum finansmanı hedefini çıkardı.

selected_news.title: Sozcu TV’ye polis baskını, yöneticiler tutuklandı
selected_news.summary: In the latest in a series of raids and arrests, another major pro-opposition Turkish broadcaster has been brought under state control. This is the third in a year.
selected_news.source_headline: Turkey takes control of opposition broadcaster Sozcu TV
selected_news.article_text: Another important opposition media outlet in Turkey has been placed under state control. On Tuesday morning, authorities raided the offices of the television broadcaster Sozcu TV and the news portal Sozcu.com.tr, and arrested several executives A trustee has also been appointed: The state deposit protection fund, TMSF, which usually administers the assets of insolvent companies, has been put in charge. Sozcu was one of the last big media companies in Turkey to regularly report critically on the government of President Recep Tayyip Erdogan A large police contingent raided the broadcaster's headquarters in Istanbul, with counterterrorism officers searching the offices. According to Sozcu, its chairwoman, Funda Tuncer Sidali, and Asim Akgul, the former chief executive of the Sozcu group, were among those arrested The broadcaster did not initially announce the appointment of the trustee on its digital channels. It did call on its audience to follow it under a new account. The leader of the main opposition party, Ozgur Ozel, declared on X: "You will never be able to prevent this nation's voice from rising, its rebellion from being heard, its cry from echoing." The Istanbul public prosecutor's office has confirmed the arrangements. It justified the investigation with claims of a suspected connection between the owner of Sozcu, Burak Akhay, and the Gülen movement. The Turkish government blames this movement, which was once allied to Erdogan, for the attempted coup in 2016, and has designated it a terrorist organization According to the investigators, Akbay is said to have used foreign bank accounts to finance two companies involved in media activities on behalf of the Gülen movement. They claim there is strong suspicion that he was able, in this way, to hold a leadership position in the organization It is not new for the Turkish state to take over media organizations by appointing trustees. Many media companies accused of being close to the Gülen movement were brought under state control in this way after the attempted coup in 2016. What is new is that for about a year now this is also happening to media seen as pro-opposition Sozcu is not the first opposition broadcaster to be targeted by the authorities. The TELEI TV channel was searched on October 24, 2025. Its editor-in-chief, Merdan Yanardag, was arrested on charges of espionage and remains in custody. The offices of Halk TV were raided on October 14 this year. There, too, a trustee was put in charge In the space of just over a year, three of the most important opposition television channels have been brought under state control. Observers see this as another step toward an increasingly authoritarian and politically isolated system Berk Esen, a political scientist with Sabanci University in Istanbul, sees these measures as a significant weakening of the opposition in the public domain Esen told DW that the government may first have acted behind the scenes and tried to bring Sozcu to heel politically. When this didn't succeed, it invoked the judiciary. Esen says Turkey is increasingly moving toward an authoritarian system. The attempt to prevent opposition organizations and media from gaining strength and influence is part of this Esen describes the opposition's success in local government elections in March 2024 as a political turning point. Since then, he says, the government has seen its chances of winning political competitions at the ballot box receding. "It's become harder for the AKP to win elections," says Esen. "That's why it's attacking the opposition and the free media both at once." Several opposition mayors have also been arrested in recent months and replaced by trustees. They include the mayor of Istanbul and presidential candidate Ekrem Imamoglu, who has been in detention since his arrest in March last year. He is regarded as one of Erdogan's most promising challengers To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video The Turkish Journalists' Association (TGC) spoke of a "black winter for press freedom," and announced its solidarity with all those affected. It described the recent developments as a serious attack on press freedom. The fact that a trustee had been appointed, first at Halk TV and now at Sozcu, showed how the media climate in Turkey has deteriorated, it said "These days, too, shall pass," the TGC declared. "When that day comes, those journalists who seek the truth today will be remembered, as will the decisions that prevent the public from hearing that truth." This article has been translated from German

selected_news.quality_narration: Salı sabahı polis, İstanbul’daki Sozcu TV merkezine baskın düzenledi ve birkaç yöneticiyi tutukladı. Devlet mevduat sigorta fonu (TMSF), kanalı yönetmek üzere mütevelli atadı. Ana muhalefet partisi lideri Özgür Özel, bu sesin susturulamayacağını belirtti.
